hits.name: @levelsio
hits.text:
Yes, I have so much time now

I honestly feel like we're entering a new time of leisure where people are just talking to their agents to steer the direction of our work, while they work in the background 24/7

Like @felixrieseberg did while building his new homepage literally on a bike ride while talking to Claude on iOS

I already kinda did this with scheduled cron jobs for years, my sites were almost fully automated, but I still had to add features or fix bugs sometimes, but now for a year or more that part is also fully automated by AI

So then we just have so much leisure time suddenly available, that we can spend time with the ppl we love, do more fun things, play games, work on our health/fitness, be outside more, etc. 

Some of that freed up time now goes into new projects, but there's a certain level of creative expression for me where it's sufficient and I am starting more and more to see I am spending that way from a computer screen too, and prefer it that way

Maybe this is the new time where we can finally live not work, as it was predicted 96 years ago by Keynes. That prediction never really came to fruition though because the automation that was invented just moved the work up to higher level (like from making actual things to financial, managerial, administrative, etc.) and people chose to just consume more, so they had to work more again!

But maybe now is different though, it definitely feels different to me

This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment.

When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company.

There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome.

Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today.

I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet.

Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

outsiders.full_text:
The AI agent fatigue is real. Unfortunately, software development has historically been measured by lines of code. And now that coding agents can generate 100x more code than humans, software engineers are expected to do 100x more in the same amount of time.

But managing AI agents is much more exhausting than writing code or even managing human developers. 

The context switching drains your mental energy. You’re constantly working on System 2 thinking, which much more exhausting than the flow of implementing a well thought feature with your headphones on. You have to keep tabs on all your agents and get them unstuck when they fall in stupid deadlocks.

And why can’t we slow down? Because the company next door is shipping 10x with Claude Code or Codex.

In the end, you reach a state of fatigue and psychosis that pushes you toward just accepting whatever the AI agent says and throw more compute and LLM tokens at the problem when they get stuck.

Fantastic for the business model of companies that sell AI tokens. Bad for your mental health and your product’s reliability.

outsiders.full_text:
Harvard's CS2680: Modern AI Systems is one of the more useful AI courses I've come across.

The lecture PDFs are free and publicly available.

What makes it worth studying is how much ground it covers, from using coding agents to building and optimizing the systems behind them.

The syllabus includes:

• How Claude Code works under the hood
• Agent loops, tools, MCP, and context management
• Multi-agent systems, memory, and reliability
• Agent evaluation and token cost optimization
• LLM inference, KV caching, and GPU optimization

The best part might be the five hands-on assignments.

You start by analyzing how Claude Code works, then build your own agent loop, optimize token usage, serve an open-weight model, and finally optimize the entire stack.

There's also a final project where students put what they've learned into practice.

If you're building AI agents, I'd bookmark this one.

Course link in the first reply 👇

virals.name: Guillermo Rauch
virals.text:
This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment.

When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company.

There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome.

Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today.

I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet.

Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

virals.name: Ben Dickson
virals.text:
The AI agent fatigue is real. Unfortunately, software development has historically been measured by lines of code. And now that coding agents can generate 100x more code than humans, software engineers are expected to do 100x more in the same amount of time.

But managing AI agents is much more exhausting than writing code or even managing human developers. 

The context switching drains your mental energy. You’re constantly working on System 2 thinking, which much more exhausting than the flow of implementing a well thought feature with your headphones on. You have to keep tabs on all your agents and get them unstuck when they fall in stupid deadlocks.

And why can’t we slow down? Because the company next door is shipping 10x with Claude Code or Codex.

In the end, you reach a state of fatigue and psychosis that pushes you toward just accepting whatever the AI agent says and throw more compute and LLM tokens at the problem when they get stuck.

Fantastic for the business model of companies that sell AI tokens. Bad for your mental health and your product’s reliability.
